title: Babur comes
hookLine: Nanak sees the cruelty of Babur's invasion at Saidpur and sings a lament that names the suffering (Asa, ang 360)

cards: Most of the travel stories so far have had a twinkle in them. Water thrown west. Feet pointed at Mecca.
A boulder stopped by a palm. Today's story has no twinkle. Remember Saidpur, the town where Lalo the carpenter shared his bread?
In the 1520s an army came over the mountains from Kabul, led by Babur, the man who would go on to found the Mughal empire. Saidpur resisted, and it was sacked.
Tradition says Nanak and Mardana were there, and were taken prisoner with the townspeople. It's easy to see terrible news and scroll past it, because it's too much. Nanak did something else.

teach.b: He sang about it. A small group of Guru Nanak's hymns, which Sikhs call the Babarvani, Babur's hymns, describe the invasion from the inside, and they are some of the most painful verses in the scripture.
One, in raga Asa, begins with Babur's army sweeping down from Khurasan and terrifying Hindustan. Then the Guru does something startling.
He turns to God and asks, in effect: so much suffering, such cries of pain, and did you feel nothing?

Another hymn describes the women of the town, whose hair had been braided and adorned with vermilion, now with their heads shaved and dust in their mouths. The palaces are empty. The proud are led away in chains.
That's what it means that he did not look away.

teach.h: HE NAMES WHO SUFFERED, AND HOW.
teach.b: He names who suffered, and how. He doesn't soften it, or turn it into a lesson about how the victims deserved it. And he argues with God about it, out loud, in a hymn sung ever since.
Sikhs hear several things in these verses. Grief, first. A witness, second: a record of what happened to ordinary people.

teach.h: A FAITH STRONG ENOUGH TO PROTEST.
teach.b: And a faith strong enough to protest, to ask God hard questions without letting go of God.
The hymns also say that the rulers of the day had forgotten their duty, and that cruelty comes back on those who do it. With this, the travel stories close.
The road that began with Mardana's music ends in the ruins of Lalo's town.

how: The Babarvani hymns are part of the Guru Granth Sahib and are sung in kirtan; Sikhs point to them as an example of the Guru speaking out against cruelty and injustice.

o: a festival marking a king's arrival in Punjab
the invasion of Saidpur, and Nanak's hymns on it

games.q: what's inside the hymns — tap the pairs.

s: the Guru's hymns avoid describing the invasion
they name the suffering plainly: the women, the ruins, the captives.
one of the Babur hymns asks God a hard question
in raga Asa: so much pain, and did you feel nothing?
Saidpur is the same town as Lalo's
the town of the carpenter's bread was the town Babur's army sacked.

games.q: you've seen a town destroyed and its people carried off. you have a voice, and people listen to your songs. what do you do?
o: sing something comforting and look ahead.
sing what you saw, and question God about it.
stay silent; it's not your place.
games.why: Nanak sang the Babarvani, naming the suffering and asking God, out loud, whether he felt nothing.

practice: Bring to mind one suffering you've looked away from: far off, a war on the news, or close, a neighbor, a relative, someone at work. Don't try to fix it; just name it, and look at it honestly for as long as the bell runs.
If you pray, you can hold it before God, even with a hard question.

wordCard.voice: Babur comes. The invasion of Saidpur, and the hymns in which Guru Nanak named the suffering and questioned God. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: Babarvani, Babur's hymns; bani is the Guru's word, set beside the invader's name.

carryVoice: Your line: he did not look away. Tomorrow, Nanak goes home and picks up a plow. Forty days now.
